title: Growing past one machine: shared-nothing, shared-disk and the cloud
goal: By the end, you can explain why adding workers to a job can make it slower, say what the machines in a cluster share and where that makes them wait, find the copy of the data that survives a crash in a cloud database, and check whether a job needs more than one machine at all.
opening:
Picture a café kitchen on a Saturday morning. Orders are piling up, so the owner calls in a second cook, and breakfast comes out almost twice as fast. A third cook helps too. By the sixth, the kitchen is slower than it was with four. The cooks queue for the one oven, and they keep stopping to ask each other who's making the toast.

We all expect more hands to mean more speed. Each new cook looks independent, so it feels as if their work should add up. It doesn't, and the reason is what the cooks share.

The last lesson, Describing load: the home timeline, measured the work coming in. It left a question open: what do we do when one machine can't carry it? In this lesson, we'll give the payments company's nightly job a bigger machine, then many machines, and watch 128 workers lose to 48. We'll find out what machines can share, and when one machine is enough. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: The payments company's nightly job adds up each shop's card payments for the day. On one worker it takes 1,025 ms (milliseconds, thousandths of a second). For 25 ms of that, a coordinator works alone: it starts the job and saves the result, and nothing else can run meanwhile. The other 1,000 ms can be shared out evenly among any number of workers. How long does the job take on 1,000 workers?
options: About 1 ms
About 26 ms
About 512 ms
Longer than on one worker
warmup.why: The 1,000 ms that can be shared out becomes 1 ms on 1,000 workers. The coordinator's 25 ms doesn't shrink at all, because only one worker can do it. That's 26 ms in total, about 39 times faster than one worker, and no number of workers can beat 1,025 / 25 = 41 times. That ceiling is called Amdahl's law, and the first section builds it. "About 1 ms" divides everything by 1,000, including the part that can't be split. A job can get slower with more workers, as the lab shows, but only when the workers also have to keep in step with each other, and this question has none of that.

sections.h: A bigger machine, and the part of the job that won't split
sections.body:
People pay for coffee, books and groceries by card, and a small payments company records every payment. Each night, it pays every shop what the shop took that day. First, a program adds up the day's payments, shop by shop: the nightly payout job. (The lab's code uses the banking word: the settlement batch.)

The job has grown. It takes 40 minutes now, and the company wants it done in 10. A computer's processor has several cores, parts that each run one stream of instructions at a time. A program can split its work into threads, paths of work that run at once, and we'll call each thread that does a share of the job a worker. So the first idea is four times the cores, and four times the workers.

That's **scaling up**, also called vertical scaling: a bigger machine. All its workers share one memory, the RAM, where a program keeps the data it's working on. So this is a **shared-memory** design, and keeping the workers in step is cheap. They can share one table of totals, guarded by a lock, a flag that lets one worker at a time change it.

AWS, Amazon's business that rents out computers over the internet, has offered one machine since December 2024 with 1,920 vCPUs and 32 TiB of memory. A vCPU is one rented thread's worth of processor, and 32 TiB (about 35 trillion bytes) is about 2,000 times a typical laptop's memory.

Two things stop you anyway. The price grows faster than the size: the biggest machines cost more per core. And four times the cores rarely do four times the work, because part of the work can't be split. Say 2.5% of the job is serial, meaning only one worker can do it. A coordinator reads the list of input files before anyone starts, and saves the result at the end, like a head cook reading out the orders.

Gene Amdahl worked out the limit in 1967. If a share σ (the Greek letter sigma) of the work is serial, N workers give a speed-up of at most 1 / (σ + (1 − σ) / N). The serial share takes as long however many workers you add; only the rest is divided by N. At σ = 2.5%, 40 workers give about 20 times, and no number of workers gives more than 1 / 0.025 = 40. That's **Amdahl's law**.

Amdahl assumed that the rest splits perfectly. Real workers also have to keep in step, like cooks asking who's making the toast. Each core keeps private copies of the memory it used recently, so when one core changes a shared value, the others must fetch it again. In the payout job, every worker sends part of its totals to every other worker, a swap called a shuffle. That cost grows with the number of pairs, N(N − 1): 4 workers make 12 pairs (counting each direction), and 40 make 1,560. So past some point, one more worker makes the whole job slower.

Neil Gunther's **Universal Scalability Law** (USL) adds that cost to Amdahl's:

```text
C(N) = N / (1 + α(N − 1) + βN(N − 1))
```

C(N) is how much work N workers do compared with one. α (alpha) is contention: the share of time spent waiting for something only one worker can use at a time, like the one oven. β (beta) is coherency: the cost of every pair of workers keeping in agreement. With β = 0, this is Amdahl's law. With any β above zero, the curve peaks at N = √((1 − α) / β) workers and then falls.

**What the workers share is where they wait. Find it before you add workers.**

The lab fits the USL to a simulated payout job on 1 to 128 workers. It finds α ≈ 0.03 and β ≈ 0.0005, a predicted peak at 45 workers and a measured best at 48. But one machine, however big, is still one machine. Next, we'll add machines, and see what they can share.

figure.caption: The lab's payout job. Amdahl's curve (dashed) knows only the serial share and keeps climbing. The USL fit (blue) also charges for every pair of workers, and turns down where the measurements do.

try.title: Find the peak, then remove the shuffle
steps: From the `labs` folder, run the demo below. It runs the payout job on 1 to 128 simulated workers, checks every run against one thread's answer, and fits the USL. Time is virtual: the code really adds up the payments, and each step adds a fixed cost to a clock, so every computer prints the same numbers.
Before it prints, predict: will 128 workers beat 64?
Run it again with `-Pargs='0 20'` at the end of the command. That makes the shuffle free: its cost per pair of workers is zero. What happens to β and to the curve?
Now try `-Pargs='2 20'`, a shuffle four times as costly per pair. Where does the peak move?

code.title: ScalingDemo.kt

try.expect:
Default costs (output trimmed):

```text
workers   time (ms)   payments/s   speed-up
      1      1025.0      975,610        1.0
      8       157.9    6,334,125        6.5
     32        76.4   13,090,547       13.4
     48        73.7   13,563,276       13.9
     64        76.2   13,122,843       13.5
    128        99.4   10,058,440       10.3

USL fit: alpha 0.0294  beta 0.000472  peak at 45 workers
measured best: 48 workers, 73.7 ms
```

128 workers are slower than 64. With `0 20`, the fit gives β = -0.000015, which is zero within the fit's error, and the speed-up keeps rising (28.5 at 128 workers): that's Amdahl's law on its own. With `2 20`, β grows about four times, to 0.001936, and the peak moves down to 22 workers. Every number comes from the virtual clock, so your output matches this one exactly.

aside.title: Where do α and β come from?
aside.body: Nobody knows them in advance, and nothing in the code tells you. You run the job at a few worker counts, say 1, 8, 32 and 64, and measure how much work it does per second at each. Then you find the α and β that make the curve pass closest to those points, which is called fitting it. The worked example below does it by hand with four numbers. The USL doesn't say why a job has its α and β, but a large β is a hint to go looking for the thing every worker touches.

sections.h: More machines: share the memory, the disk or nothing
sections.body:
When one machine isn't enough, you add machines: scaling out, or horizontal scaling. A group of machines that work as one system is a cluster, and each machine in it is a node. The big question is what the nodes share, and the kitchen has all three answers.

**Shared memory** is the single machine from the last section: one kitchen with more cooks. Keeping in step is cheap, but if the one machine breaks, everything stops. It's a single point of failure: a part whose fault alone takes the whole system down.

**Shared disk** is several kitchens, each with its own stove, sharing one pantry down the hall. Here, several machines, each with its own processors and memory, read and write the same disks over a fast storage network (sold as a SAN or a NAS). The best-known example is Oracle RAC. Oracle sells a popular database, a program that stores data and answers questions about it, and RAC runs one database on several machines. Each machine runs a copy of the database program, called an instance, and every instance opens the same data files, so any of them can answer any question.

The pantry needs rules: two cooks can't both take the last bag of flour. A database keeps its data in blocks of a few kilobytes, and two instances must not change one block at once. So RAC keeps a global lock manager, a referee that hands out permission to change each block. When instance 2 needs a block that instance 1 has changed, a feature called Cache Fusion sends it from instance 1's memory over a private network link. That traffic is shared disk's β. It's why shared-disk clusters stay small, a handful of nodes, used mostly to keep running when one machine fails.

**Shared nothing** is a chain of restaurants, each with its own pantry, that coordinate by phone. Each node has its own processors, memory and disks, and nodes work together only by sending messages over an ordinary network. The data is split into partitions, pieces that each belong to one node; the Partitioning track builds them.

The nodes can be cheap, ordinary machines, added one at a time. They can spread across racks (cabinets of machines that share power) and availability zones (separate data centres in one cloud region), so the cluster survives losing one of them. Kafka, a program that stores streams of messages for other programs to read, works this way; each of its machines is called a broker. So does PostgreSQL, a free database program, when it runs with a standby, a second machine that keeps its own copy, fed with every change.

The price comes in two parts. Something must decide where every piece of data lives, and send each request there. And every exchange between nodes is a network message, which can be lost, delayed or delivered twice. Here the restaurant picture breaks. A dropped phone call is obvious, and you call back. A lost message can leave a node unable to tell whether the other side got it and acted on it. The Faults, time and truth track takes that apart.

The lab's payout job is shared nothing too. Each worker adds up its own slice, and the shuffle sends each shop's partial totals to the worker that owns that shop.

Most real systems mix the three: each Kafka broker is a shared-memory computer inside a shared-nothing cluster. And the cloud has brought shared disk back. Next, we'll see how.

try.title: Sort five systems by what they share
steps: For each system, say which design it uses (shared memory, shared disk or shared nothing), and name the one thing its nodes or threads wait for: Oracle RAC; one PostgreSQL server on one machine; a PostgreSQL server with a standby; Kafka on three brokers; Redis Cluster on six machines. (Redis is a program that keeps data in memory, often used as a cache, and Redis Cluster spreads that data over several machines.)
Then pick one of them and say what happens when one of its machines dies.
try.expect: Oracle RAC is shared disk: the instances wait for the referee (the global lock manager) and for blocks sent by Cache Fusion. One PostgreSQL server is shared memory: its workers wait for locks and for room in its shared memory, and the machine is a single point of failure. A server with a standby is shared nothing: the standby keeps its own copy on its own disk, and waits for the stream of changes (PostgreSQL's log of changes, called the WAL) sent over the network. Kafka and Redis Cluster are shared nothing too: each partition of Kafka's logs, or each range of Redis keys (the names its values are stored under), lives on its own nodes, and a client must find the right node. If a Kafka broker dies, another broker that holds a copy of each of its partitions takes over. If the single PostgreSQL machine dies, everything waits until it's back.

sections.h: The cloud brings back the shared disk: storage apart from compute
sections.body:
A rented cloud computer usually comes with a local disk, and the disk disappears with it. It's gone when the computer fails or moves to another physical machine. A network disk such as Amazon EBS survives, because it lives on Amazon's storage machines, but every read or write becomes a network call.

That gets costly fast, because a database writes each change twice. It first appends a short note to its log, a file it only ever adds to at the end, so a crash loses nothing. Later it writes the changed pages, the blocks its tables are stored in, often 8 KB each. Keep a mirror in a second zone, and each transaction (one change the database must make safely, such as recording one payment) turns into many network writes.

Amazon measured the cost in its 2017 paper on Aurora, its cloud database built from MySQL, a popular free database program. Both ran a 30-minute test of writes only, on the same size of machine. Mirrored MySQL completed 780,000 transactions at 7.4 I/Os each, where an I/O is one read or write to storage. Aurora completed 27,378,000 at 0.95 I/Os each: 35 times the transactions, with 7.7 times fewer I/Os each, while keeping six copies of the data.

Aurora's trick is that **the log is the database**. The database instance sends only redo log records, the short notes that say what each change did, to a separate fleet of storage machines. The storage machines build the pages from those notes themselves, so pages never cross the network on a write. The data is cut into 10 GB segments, and each segment has six copies, two in each of three availability zones. A write counts once four copies have it, and a read needs three. Those numbers are quorums: how many copies must answer before an operation counts. The stepper shows what they buy.

In the kitchen, this is a central warehouse that delivers to kitchens, which keep only today's ingredients. If a kitchen burns down, nothing is lost. The warehouse holds the durable copy, the one that survives a crash, and a kitchen's shelf is only a cache, a quick copy that can be refilled.

Newer designs use object storage as the warehouse. Object storage, such as Amazon S3, keeps files, called objects, by name, cheaply and safely. Kafka, for one, has an accepted design, the proposal KIP-1150, for diskless topics: named logs whose data lives in object storage, with the brokers' disks used only as a cache. The reason is money: AWS charges $0.02 per GiB (about a billion bytes) that crosses between zones, and ordinary Kafka copies every byte across zones. The price is slower writes.

**Where is the durable copy, and what is only a cache? Ask that first, of any system.**

| System | Durable copy | Only a cache |
|---|---|---|
| Aurora | 6 copies of each 10 GB segment, across 3 zones | the instance's memory |
| Kafka diskless topic | object storage | the brokers' disks |

Both designs still have you choose and pay for machines. Next come two ideas that take even that away, or split the program itself.

frames.say: The storage fleet copies the segment from a surviving copy onto a new machine. A 10 GB segment takes about **10 seconds** over a 10 Gbit/s link, so the time in which one more failure could hurt is seconds long. With four copies again, writes resume. That's why Aurora cuts the data into small segments: how often disks fail isn't up to it, but how fast it repairs them is.

try.title: Check Aurora's quorums by trying every case
steps: Run the demo below from the `labs` folder. It tries every possible set of lost copies, from none to all six, and counts the cases where writes (4 healthy copies) and reads (3) still work.
Predict first: there are 20 ways to lose three copies. In how many can you still write? In how many can you still read?
Change `WRITE_QUORUM` to 3 and run it again. Writes now survive one more lost copy. Look at the two overlap checks at the end. What could go wrong?

code.title: QuorumDemo.kt

try.expect:
Output trimmed (the rows for 5 and 6 lost copies are all zeros):

```text
lost  cases  writes ok  reads ok
   0      1          1         1
   1      6          6         6
   2     15         15        15
   3     20          0        20
   4     15          0         0

zone a fails                 alive 4  writes yes  reads yes
zone a fails, then c2 dies   alive 3  writes no   reads yes
zones a and b fail           alive 2  writes no   reads no

every read quorum overlaps every write quorum: true   (4 + 3 > 6 is true)
every two write quorums overlap:               true   (4 + 4 > 6 is true)
```

Any two losses, a whole zone included, leave writes working, and any three leave reads working. With a write quorum of 3, the three-loss row says `20 20`, and both checks print `false`. Two writes could each be acknowledged by three different copies (3 + 3 is not more than 6), so two writes that disagree could both "succeed". And a read of three copies could miss the newest write entirely. The Replication track builds quorums properly.

sections.h: Renting by the request, and splitting the program: serverless and microservices
sections.body:
Two more ways to grow past one machine are about money and people more than data. The first is **serverless**, also called functions as a service. Think of a catering firm that sends cooks only when orders come in. You give a cloud provider, a company such as AWS, a function, a piece of code that handles one request, and never pick a machine. The provider starts copies of it as requests arrive, and bills you for the time they run. When nobody calls, you pay nothing.

The price comes as limits. A function may run only so long, and only with the languages and libraries the provider supports. And there are **cold starts**: the first request to a new copy waits while the provider starts it. It's the first order of the day, waiting while the cook drives over. Since 1 August 2025, AWS Lambda, Amazon's serverless service, bills for that start-up time too. AWS says cold starts happen on under 1% of calls.

Serverless suits light work that comes in bursts. Steady, heavy work can cost far more. In 2023, the team behind Prime Video, Amazon's video streaming service, moved one service off serverless steps into one program, and cut its cost by over 90%.

The second idea is **microservices**: split one application into small programs, called services, that talk over the network. Each owns one job, one API (the list of requests it accepts) and one database, and one team runs it. Think of a food hall, where each stall has its own kitchen and staff. A service can release a new version on its own schedule and change how it works inside, as long as its API stays the same. Services avoid sharing a database, because then its table layout would become part of every service's API.

Testing one service needs the others running. Every service needs its own releases, monitoring and someone to fix it at night. Changing an API breaks its callers, often late. And keeping data consistent across services becomes the application's problem, because one transaction, a group of changes that happens completely or not at all, can't cover several services' databases. The Encoding and Transactions tracks take both problems on.

So microservices answer a problem about people: letting many teams move without waiting for each other. For a payments company with twelve teams, that's worth a lot; for three teams, it's usually overhead. On their own, they aren't how a system scales. What scales is independence, and splitting one database into partitions gives you that too.

Both ideas still assume that you need many machines. Next, we'll ask whether you do.

sections.h: When one machine is enough: the COST of a cluster
sections.body:
A speed-up curve compares a system with itself. Our payout job's curve says that 48 workers do 13.9 times the work of one cluster worker. It never says whether we needed the cluster at all. In 2015, Frank McSherry, Michael Isard and Derek Murray proposed a measure that does: **COST**, the Configuration that Outperforms a Single Thread. It's how much hardware a system needs before it beats one well-written program on one thread.

They took published results for systems that process graphs, sets of points joined by lines, and ran the same problems on one thread on a 2014 laptop. The graph was Twitter's: 41.7 million accounts and 1.47 billion follows.

The first problem was 20 rounds of PageRank, the method Google first used to rank web pages, here ranking accounts by who follows them. Spark, a program that runs big data jobs across many computers, took 857 s on 128 cores. GraphX, a part of Spark built for graphs, took 419 s on 128 cores. One thread reading from an SSD (a fast disk with no moving parts) took 300 s, and 110 s with the follows in a smarter order, in memory.

The second problem was finding connected components: groups of accounts joined by any chain of follows. The method that suits these frameworks took 1,784 s on Spark and 251 s on GraphX, both on 128 cores. One thread running union-find, an older method that does far less work but doesn't split as neatly, took **15 s**. GraphX never beat one thread at PageRank: by the authors' reading, its COST is unbounded.

Why so bad? Frameworks pay for every record (turning it into a general-purpose row, packing it into bytes to send, scheduling it) and for every round of coordination. And they push you toward methods that split well, not methods that do little work. Oddly, extra work that splits evenly makes a speed-up curve look better, because one worker is so slow to begin with.

In the lab, a plain loop with a map (a table from each shop to its total) adds up a million payments in 100 ms on one thread. The simulated cluster pays ten times as much per payment, plus a start-up and a shuffle. It needs 16 workers to beat one thread, and its best is 73.7 ms at 48 workers. Make the shuffle cost 2 ms per pair of workers, and no cluster size ever wins.

**A cluster must beat one good thread before it's worth anything. Measure that first.**

One machine today has up to 1,920 vCPUs and 32 TiB of memory. Small databases that run inside another program, such as DuckDB and SQLite, now handle data that needed clusters ten years ago. Jordan Tigani, who worked on BigQuery, Google's cloud warehouse, estimated in 2023 that most of its customers stored under a terabyte in total. There are still good reasons to spread out: data that outgrows a machine, several terabytes arriving each day, surviving the loss of a zone, users on several continents. Each one pays what this lesson measured, in α, in β and in messages that go missing.

try.title: Find the COST, then break it
steps: Look at the last line of the output from the first Try it: the COST of the default cluster.
Run the demo with `-Pargs='0.5 200'`: the same shuffle, but a start-up of 200 ms instead of 20 ms, which is still short for a real cluster framework. Predict the COST before you run it.
Which of the cluster's costs would you cut first to make it win, and what would that do to α and β?
try.expect:
Default costs: `COST: 16 workers to beat one thread (99.7 ms)`, against 100.0 ms for one thread.

With a 200 ms start-up:

```text
USL fit: alpha 0.1744  beta 0.000402  peak at 45 workers
measured best: 48 workers, 253.7 ms
COST: unbounded, no number of workers beats one thread
```

The start-up is serial, so it raises α (from 0.029 to 0.174) and puts a floor of 200 ms under every run: no number of workers gets below the 100 ms of one thread. Cutting serial work lowers α. Cutting the cost per payment lowers the whole cluster curve, and that's what lowers the COST most.

refs.title: McSherry, Isard and Murray, Scalability! But at what COST? (HotOS 2015)
Jordan Tigani, Big Data is Dead (MotherDuck)

mistake: Adding workers without measuring the curve. A slow job gets more threads or more machines, and gets slower, because the work waits on one shared thing: a lock on one busy record, one database's processor, a shuffle in which everybody talks to everybody. People expect parallel work to be free, because each new worker looks independent. The fix is to measure the work done at four or five worker counts, fit the USL, and read α and β. A big α means: find the serial step and shrink it. A big β means: find what every worker keeps in agreement, and stop sharing it. Only then add workers, and stop well before the peak.

a.label: one thread
a.title: runOnOneThread: 1,000,000 payments in 100 ms

b.label: simulated cluster
b.title: runOnCluster: phases, each as slow as its slowest worker
b.src:
startup        20 ms              serial (alpha)
map            1,000 ns x payments / N
shuffle        0.5 ms x (N - 1)   every pair connects (beta)
               + 500 ns per partial sum sent or received
commit         5 ms               serial (alpha)

N = 16: 99.7 ms   N = 48: 73.7 ms   N = 128: 99.4 ms

compare.note: Both compute exactly the same totals; the lab checks that. The loop on the left has no start-up, no shuffle and no framework cost per payment, so the cluster needs 16 workers to catch up with it. The cluster's own costs map onto the USL. The start-up and the commit (saving the result) are the serial share, α. The shuffle, paid for every pair of workers, is the coherency cost β that makes 128 workers slower than 48.

worked.title: Fit the USL to four measurements by hand

steps.say: Take four measurements from the demo: how many payments the job handles per second at each number of workers, N. Divide each by the one-worker number to get C, how many times the work of one worker N workers do.

The USL is a curve, and a straight line is easier to fit than a curve. So rearrange it into one. For each N above 1, compute x = N − 1 and z = (N / C − 1) / (N − 1). If the USL holds, the points (x, z) lie on the line z = (α + β) + βx.

Draw the straight line that passes closest to the three points. The standard way is called least squares, and the lab's hints give its two formulas. The line's slope is β, and its intercept, where it crosses x = 0, is α + β.
Now predict the peak, and check the fit at a worker count you didn't use. The fit says 13.57 million payments a second at 48 workers. The demo measured 13.56 million.
steps.code:
peak = sqrt((1 - alpha) / beta) = sqrt(0.97055 / 0.000473) ≈ 45 workers

fun usl(n: Int, alpha: Double, beta: Double) =
    n / (1.0 + alpha * (n - 1) + beta * n * (n - 1.0))
975_610 * usl(48, 0.02945, 0.000473)    // ≈ 13.57 million/s

lab.title: Fit the scaling curve, then find the COST
steps: Run the tests once from the `labs` folder with the command above. Tests are small programs that check your code and say what's wrong. All 7 fail with `NotImplementedError`, Kotlin's way of saying a function's body is still a `TODO`.

Read `Settlement.kt`. It's finished: the payout job (the settlement batch, in the code) on one thread and on a simulated shared-nothing cluster. Every step adds its cost to a virtual clock. The totals are real, so the tests can check that both versions give the same answer.
In `Scaling.kt`, write `amdahl`, `usl` and `uslPeak`. Each is one line, and the comment above each function gives its formula.

Write `fitUsl`. Turn each measurement into a point (N − 1, (N / C − 1) / (N − 1)), fit a straight line by least squares, and read β from the slope and α from the intercept minus the slope. One test feeds it exact USL data and expects α and β back to nine decimal places. Another feeds it the measured job and checks the predicted peak.
Write `cost`, then run the tests until all 7 pass. The last test finds the cluster's COST (16 workers), and shows that with a slower shuffle no number of workers wins.
hints: Turn numbers into `Double` with `toDouble()` before you divide. `n / c` works because `c` is already a `Double`, but `(n - 1)` on its own is an `Int`, a whole number.

Least squares for a line: slope = Σ(x − x̄)(z − z̄) / Σ(x − x̄)², and intercept = z̄ − slope × x̄. Σ means "add up over all the points", and x̄ and z̄ are the averages of x and z. You don't need a library.
`uslPeak` must return `Double.POSITIVE_INFINITY` when β is zero or less. Without a coherency cost, the curve never turns down.
`cost` is `(1..maxWorkers).firstOrNull { clusterSeconds(it) < singleThreadSeconds }`. Note the strict `<`: the same time doesn't count as beating one thread.

drill.title: Fit the USL from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write `fitUsl(measured: Map<Int, Double>): UslFit`. It takes the work done per second at each number of workers (N = 1 included) and returns α, β and the one-worker number. Write down the straight line you fit before you write the code.

recap: Scaling up means one bigger machine, whose workers share its memory; today one machine reaches 1,920 vCPUs and 32 TiB. It stops paying when the price grows faster than the size, and when the serial part caps the speed-up (Amdahl's law).
The Universal Scalability Law, C(N) = N / (1 + α(N − 1) + βN(N − 1)), adds the cost of every pair of workers keeping in step. The work done peaks at √((1 − α) / β) workers and then falls.

Shared memory shares one machine's RAM. Shared disk shares the storage behind a referee for every block (Oracle RAC). Shared nothing shares only the network, and has to split the data into partitions.

Cloud systems keep storage apart from compute. Aurora sends only log records to six copies in three zones (4 to write, 3 to read), and Kafka's diskless topics keep their data in object storage. Ask of any system where the durable copy is, and what is only a cache.

Serverless sells paying per use, at the price of limits and cold starts. Microservices let many teams work without waiting for each other, at the price of running many programs and keeping their data consistent.

The limit: more machines pay only when they beat one good thread. COST measures that, and many published systems needed hundreds of cores or never got there, so measure it before you spread a job out.
closing:
We started in a kitchen where the sixth cook made breakfast slower. The payout job did the same: 48 workers beat 128, because every pair of workers had to talk. What the workers share is where they wait, and a cluster still has to beat one good thread.

Find out how many workers your own computer offers. On a Mac, run `sysctl -n hw.ncpu` in Terminal; on Linux, run `nproc`; on Windows, look at the Performance tab of Task Manager. That's how far one machine goes before anything has to cross a network.

Next, we'll ask what makes a system easy to live with for years, and why most of its cost comes after it first works.

quiz.q: Measurements of a job fit the USL with α = 0.02 and β = 0.0002. At about how many workers does the work done per second peak?
options: Around 70 workers
Around 50 workers
Around 4,900 workers
It never peaks; it keeps climbing toward 1 / α = 50 times
quiz.why: The peak is at √((1 − α) / β) = √(0.98 / 0.0002) = √4,900 = 70 workers. 4,900 forgets the square root. "It never peaks" is Amdahl's law, which is the USL with β = 0. Any β above zero, however small, makes the curve turn down in the end.

quiz.q: Oracle RAC runs one database on three machines that share the same data files. Two of the machines keep changing the same block, the one that holds a busy shop's balance. Where does that cost show up?
options: Nowhere: each machine keeps its own copy of the block on its own disk
In messages between the machines: asking the referee for permission, and sending the block itself from one machine's memory to the other's
In the network between the card readers and the database
In Kafka copying data between zones
quiz.why: RAC is shared disk: the machines share the data files, not copies of them. Before one machine changes a block that another has changed, the global lock manager, RAC's referee, must give it permission, and Cache Fusion sends the block over the private link. A busy block bouncing between machines is the coherency cost, β. "Each machine keeps its own copy" describes shared nothing.

quiz.q: Aurora keeps six copies of each 10 GB segment of its data, two in each of three zones. A write needs 4 copies to answer, and a read needs 3. Zone b goes down, and then one copy in zone c fails. What still works?
options: Reads and writes, because three copies are still healthy
Reads, but not writes, until a copy is rebuilt
Neither, and the last writes are lost
Writes, but not reads
quiz.why: Three healthy copies are enough for a read (3) but not for a write (4). Nothing saved is lost: every write was acknowledged by four copies, and any three copies include at least one of those four, because 3 + 4 > 6. Once the segment is copied onto a new machine (about 10 s for 10 GB), four copies exist again and writes resume.

quiz.q: A framework's speed grows exactly with its cores from 16 to 512 cores (twice the cores, half the time), and it finishes a job in 10 s on 512 cores. One well-written thread does the same job in 60 s. What is the framework's COST for this job?
options: 86 cores
512 cores
6 cores
1 core, because it scales perfectly
quiz.why: Perfect scaling means the time is 10 s × 512 / N = 5,120 / N seconds. That beats 60 s when N is above 85.3, so the COST is 86 cores. 512 is only the largest size measured. 6 cores comes from 60 / 10, which compares the times without looking at the hardware each one took. A perfect speed-up curve says nothing about how slow the first core is.

quiz.q: Why does Aurora put two copies in each of three availability zones, and not three copies in each of two?
options: Three zones are cheaper than two
A zone fails as a unit, taking all its copies at once; with 2, 2 and 2, a lost zone leaves four copies, enough to keep writing
Disks in different zones fail at different rates
Reads must come from three different zones
quiz.why: Faults aren't always independent, as Faults, failures and the people who run systems showed. When a zone goes down, every copy in it goes at once. With 3 and 3 across two zones, losing a zone leaves three copies, one short of the write quorum of four. With 2, 2 and 2, losing any zone leaves four, so writes carry on, and even a zone plus one more copy leaves three for reads. The reason is faults that strike together, not different failure rates per zone.

flashcards.front: Amdahl's law: the speed-up on N workers when a share σ of the work is serial?
flashcards.back: 1 / (σ + (1 − σ) / N). It never passes 1 / σ: with 5% serial, the speed-up stops at 20 times.

flashcards.front: What do α and β mean in the Universal Scalability Law?
flashcards.back: α is contention: waiting for something only one worker can use at a time. β is coherency: the cost of every pair of workers keeping in agreement. The curve peaks at √((1 − α) / β).

flashcards.front: Shared disk or shared nothing: what do the machines share?
flashcards.back: Shared disk: the storage, so they need a referee that hands out permission to change each block. Shared nothing: only the network; each machine owns its own partitions on its own disks.

flashcards.front: Aurora's storage: how many copies, and what are the quorums?
flashcards.back: 10 GB segments, 6 copies of each, 2 in each of 3 zones. Writes need 4 copies, reads 3. Writes survive a lost zone; reads survive a zone plus one more copy.

flashcards.front: What does "the log is the database" mean in Aurora?
flashcards.back: The database sends only redo log records, short notes of what changed, to storage, and the storage machines build the pages themselves. Pages never cross the network on a write.
The Configuration that Outperforms a Single Thread: how much hardware a system needs before it beats one well-written program on one thread. It can be unbounded.

flashcards.front: Why did Kafka accept a design for diskless topics (KIP-1150)?
flashcards.back: Copying every byte between availability zones costs money (on AWS, $0.02 per GiB). Keeping the data in object storage avoids that, at the price of slower writes.

terms.plain: Handling more work with a bigger machine.
Handling more work with more machines.
Several machines, each with its own processors and memory, that read and write the same storage.
Machines that each have their own processors, memory and disks, and work together only by sending messages.
A formula for how much work N workers do, which charges for waiting (α) and for keeping in step (β).
How many copies must answer before a read or a write counts.
The extra wait when a serverless service starts a new copy of your function.
The hardware a system needs before it beats one well-written thread.

explain_back.prompt: A friend wants to move the nightly payout job from one big computer to 64 computers "so it scales". Explain what you'd measure first, and why more computers could make the job slower.
explain_back.answer: First I'd time one well-written thread on the same data, because the cluster has to beat that before it's worth anything. That comparison is its COST, and published systems often needed hundreds of cores to beat one thread, mostly because they pay extra for every record they handle. Then I'd measure how much work the cluster does at a few sizes and fit the Universal Scalability Law. α is the part only one worker can do, like starting the job and saving the result, and it caps the speed-up, as Amdahl's law says. β is the cost of the computers keeping in step, like a shuffle in which every computer talks to every other. It grows with the number of pairs, so past the peak, √((1 − α) / β), each extra computer makes the job slower. If one big computer, or a better method, finishes in time, that's simpler to run and has fewer ways to fail.

deeper.body:
**Where the USL comes from.** Neil Gunther introduced the model in the early 1990s for database programs on machines with many processors, and later named it the Universal Scalability Law. It comes from fitting measurements, not from a proof. It doesn't say why a system has its α or β, only that most measured curves fit the shape. That's also its use. A fitted β well above zero tells you to look for the thing every worker touches, and a fit to small measurements can predict the peak before anyone buys the big cluster.

**Why Snowflake left shared nothing.** Snowflake sells a data warehouse, a database for analysis, that keeps its tables as files in S3. The 2016 Snowflake paper names three problems with tying data to the machines that compute on it, in the cloud. Different work wants different hardware: a big load wants fast disks and network, a complex question wants processors. Resizing the cluster means moving data on the same machines that are busy answering questions. And upgrading without stopping is harder when every machine holds data nobody else has. Its answer was shared storage in S3, with many separate groups of compute machines, called virtual warehouses, each keeping a cache of what it reads on local SSDs. Files are assigned to machines with consistent hashing (a way to spread items over machines so that adding one moves few of them; the Partitioning track builds it), so resizing a warehouse moves no data, and several warehouses can read the same tables at once without slowing each other.

**Neon, piece by piece.** Neon, a service that runs PostgreSQL in the cloud, keeps no data on the compute machine. The log goes to a few machines called safekeepers, which agree on it with Paxos, a method for a group of machines to agree on one value even when some of them fail (the Consistency and consensus track covers it). A commit counts once a quorum of safekeepers has it. Pageservers rebuild pages from the log, object storage keeps the history, and the compute can shut down to zero when nobody uses it. So its durable copy is the log on the safekeepers, then object storage, and the compute's memory and local disk are only a cache.

**Object storage gets faster.** S3 Express One Zone is a kind of S3 that answers in single-digit milliseconds, inside one zone. In April 2025 its storage price in us-east-1 fell from $0.16 to $0.11 per GB-month (a gigabyte kept for a month).

**Aurora's numbers in perspective.** The 35 times more transactions came from a write-only test against MySQL mirrored across zones on EBS, the setup that suffers most from sending pages. Aurora still writes six copies of every log record. It sends far less data per write, sends the six writes at once, and needs only the fastest four to answer. So one slow storage machine, a gray failure in the terms of Faults, failures and the people who run systems, doesn't slow commits down.

**Cold starts in Java.** For Java functions, AWS Lambda's SnapStart takes a snapshot of a copy after it has started up, and restores that snapshot for new copies instead of starting each one from scratch.

**Traffic between zones shapes designs.** KIP-1150 quotes $0.02 per GiB for traffic between zones on AWS and $0.01 on Google Cloud, and nothing on Azure. A Kafka topic with three copies in three zones sends every byte written across zones twice for its copies, and often again to readers in other zones. At a few hundred MB/s, that adds up to a larger bill than the brokers themselves. That's why diskless designs, which let object storage do the copying, appeared first as commercial products and then as a Kafka proposal.

**A smarter order.** The 110 s PageRank run in the COST paper stored the graph's follows along a Hilbert curve, an order that keeps follows between accounts with nearby numbers next to each other, so each read from memory brings in more useful data.

**The biggest machine, in detail.** The AWS machine from the first section, the `u7inh-32tb.480xlarge`, is one server with 16 processor chips and a 200 Gbit/s (gigabits per second) network link.

**Tiered storage before diskless.** Kafka 3.9 (November 2024) made tiered storage ready for real use: old parts of a log move to object storage, and the brokers keep only the recent part on their own disks. Diskless topics go one step further and keep everything there.

**Serverless as a label.** The word now also labels any cloud service that grows on its own and bills by use, such as BigQuery or some services that run Kafka for you.

**The Prime Video case.** In 2023, Amazon's Prime Video team described a service that checked the quality of video streams. It was built from AWS Step Functions steps (a service that runs a chain of small cloud steps) that handed video frames to each other through S3. Moving it into a single program on rented machines (EC2 and ECS, Amazon's services for that) cut its cost by over 90%. Commentators noted that this was one service, and that most of the savings came from paying per step and per S3 request, so it says little about splitting programs in general.

**GraphLab's COST.** By the COST paper's reading, GraphLab, another graph system, needed 512 cores to beat one thread at PageRank.
